chunks: Specifying an ESC. The question: How do you spec an ESC?
Specifying an ESC means matching it to the motor and the battery.
Check that its voltage rating covers the battery, that its current rating covers what the motor really draws (plus margin), and that it speaks the right command protocol.
Then check the extras: whether it can switch fast enough for the motor's speed, the BEC, size, cooling and protections.
It is like buying an extension cord or power strip. You add up what will be plugged in, then choose one rated well above that. A cord rated just at the limit will overheat.
The same goes for an ESC: rate it above the measured load, not the number on the motor's label.
The analogy has a gap: an ESC can also be destroyed by too much voltage, not just too much current.
Spec an ESC from the application inward: battery and motor determine the electrical needs; features and packaging follow; bench validation closes the loop.
Any failure at the end sends you back to a larger rating or better cooling.
Cell count (S): the number of battery cells in series. A 4S LiPo is 4 times 4. 2 volts = 16. 8 volts fully charged.
Continuous current rating: the current the ESC can carry without overheating. Burst rating: a short-term current limit, only meaningful with stated test conditions.
Protocol: the throttle language, such as DShot. BEC: the built-in 5 volts supply for outside electronics.
A 4S pack is 4 times 4. 2 = 16. 8 volts, so the ESC must be rated for at least 4S. Suppose you measure 38 amps at full throttle. Add 25 to 50% margin: 38 times 1.
25 about 48 amps and 38 times 1. 5 = 57 amps. So pick an ESC in the 50 amps class or above.

Then check speed: a motor with a 34,000 rpm (revolutions per minute) no-load speed and 7 pole pairs (north-south magnet pairs) needs its coils switched through 34,000 times 7 / 60 about 4,000 cycles per second (4 kilohertz).
The ESC must handle that. That is the whole idea: voltage, current, protocol and speed must all match.
"I start from the battery and motor. Voltage: the ESC must be rated for the pack's maximum, 16. 8 volts for 4S, with margin.
Current: take the motor's measured full-throttle current on the real prop, and choose an ESC with continuous rating 25 to 50% above it, checking burst duration.
Then compatibility: protocol like DShot, firmware that supports the motor's electrical rpm, BEC if needed, protections, telemetry.
Finally the practical side, size, cooling, wires and I'd verify temperature on a bench test."
